analysis.one_liner: Banned disproportionately exposing minority and low-income communities to hazardous substances and funded community health assessments.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Health Subcommittee in April 2007 and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the 110th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The Community Environmental Equity Act would have made it illegal for any company or facility handling hazardous substances — drinking-water contaminants, pesticides, known carcinogens, regulated chemicals, hazardous waste, or air pollutants — to disproportionately expose a person or community to those substances because of race, color, national origin, or income. The government could enforce this by denying or revoking the authorization a facility needs to operate. It also would have given small grants ($1 million a year) to community organizations and health centers to measure the environmental health of their own neighborhoods. The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Health Subcommittee until the two-year session of Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents of low-income, minority, and urban communities that the bill's findings described as overburdened with polluting facilities — waste transfer stations, power plants, superfund sites, brownfields, and toxic release sites — would have gained a legal right against disproportionate exposure, backed by permit denial or revocation. Community organizations and health centers in those neighborhoods would have received federal grants to document local health impacts and identify harmful exposures.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low-income and minority communities near polluting facilities

how_it_helps.text: It would have barred any entity handling regulated hazardous substances from disproportionately exposing a person or community to them on the basis of race, color, national origin, or economic status, with enforcement including denial or termination of the authorization needed to work with those substances.
It required entities to address actual or potential disproportionate exposure before seeking state or local permits, moving environmental-justice concerns into the permitting process itself.

It authorized $1 million a year (fiscal 2008-2010) in grants to community-based organizations and community health centers to build neighborhood health profiles, assess the health consequences of proposed development, and identify harmful exposures, with no more than 10 percent going to administrative costs.

The bill cited evidence that low-income and minority communities are overburdened with polluting facilities and often lack the resources to defend themselves, and that asthma affects over 15 million people, including 6.5 million children.

analysis.who_pays: Companies and facilities that handle, treat, store, transport, or dispose of regulated hazardous substances — chemical makers, waste handlers, utilities, and pesticide users — would have faced a new prohibition and enforcement regime, including the potential loss of their authorization to operate, plus the cost of assessing and addressing disparate exposures before permitting.

drawbacks.text: The core prohibition was broad and vague: it covered nearly every regulated contaminant, pesticide, and chemical, and barred any 'disproportionate exposure' tied to race or economic status without defining how disparity would be measured, which could have created major legal uncertainty for manufacturers, utilities, and waste handlers.

Enforcement could mean denial or termination of an entity's authorization to handle covered substances at all — a sweeping penalty that could shut down facilities, with job and cost consequences the bill did not address.
The bill authorized only $1 million a year for community health impact grants, a small fraction of the cost of the environmental monitoring and health profiling it envisioned.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — a legal right not to be disproportionately poisoned because of race or income, plus modest community health funding — was real but the bill's design had serious weaknesses. The "disproportionate exposure" standard was vague and swept in essentially every federally regulated substance, and enforcement by stripping an entity's authorization to handle those substances outright could have been a blunt instrument with a wide compliance burden for manufacturers, utilities, and waste handlers, some of it falling on operations far from the overburdened communities the bill targeted. Even so, the bill never got a hearing or a vote in committee, so those tradeoffs were never tested or refined; the country got neither the protection nor the fixes.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the Energy and Commerce Committee and then its Health Subcommittee in April 2007, and no hearing, markup, or vote ever happened before the two-year session ended.

narrative.text: The House referred H.R. 1972 to the Committee on Energy and Commerce on April 19, 2007, the day it was introduced.
On April 20, 2007, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, which was the last action ever taken on the bill.
The bill died at the end of the 110th Congress on January 3, 2009, without a committee report, a floor vote, or any companion Senate action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that handle, store, transport, or dispose of hazardous substances never had to comply with a new exposure-discrimination rule or face permit revocation; low-income and minority residents near polluting facilities gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Hazardous-substance handlers who avoided new rules

for.name: Rep. Nydia Velazquez
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Community Environmental Equity Act on April 19, 2007.

for.name: Reps. Alcee Hastings, Sheila Jackson-Lee, Jose Serrano, and Donna Christensen
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's four original cosponsors, all Democrats.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral under Chair John Dingell (D-MI)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day of introduction and never held a hearing, markup, or vote; it was the last committee to touch the bill.

against.name: Subcommittee on Health
against.role: Subcommittee of the House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on April 20, 2007 and took no further action; the referral was the bill's final congressional action.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the bill's sponsor and all four cosponsors were Democrats, and the Democratic-run Energy and Commerce Committee gave it no action, so partisan positions beyond sponsorship were never tested.

industries.note: The bill covered every chemical regulated under the Toxic Substances Control Act and every known or probable carcinogen, and made a disparate-exposure claim grounds for losing authorization to operate. This was the industry the bill was most directly aimed at.

Hazardous waste handlers would have faced a new requirement to prove they were not disproportionately burdening minority or low-income neighborhoods before getting permits, and risked termination of authorization to handle waste.

industries.industry: Power plants and other air polluters
industries.note: Any regulated air pollutant counted as a covered substance, so facilities sited in overburdened communities would have faced a new civil-rights-style line of attack on their permits.
Registered pesticides were covered substances, extending the exposure-discrimination rule to agricultural and commercial pesticide use.

industries.industry: Community health centers and community-based organizations
industries.note: They would have received federal grants to build health impact profiles and document exposures in their neighborhoods, and the bill specified they must be local or partnered locally.
